messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Doctor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Breathlessness): Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Violence: Violence
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Chukwu's Vigil

Chukwu was twenty years old and already a doctor—a fact that had once meant everything to him. He had immigrated from Nigeria at sixteen, worked through secondary school while his mother cleaned houses, and had been admitted to medical school on a full scholarship. His white coat hung in his apartment in Boston, unworn for three weeks now. He could not bring himself to put it on again.

The bombing had happened eight months earlier during a humanitarian mission in a conflict zone in West Africa. Chukwu had volunteered through a medical NGO, wanting to work in his ancestral region, to give back. The clinic had been a concrete structure with a tin roof, set in a town whose name he could still see written on the supply manifests he had helped unload that morning. He remembered the heat. He remembered the smell of antiseptic and dust. He remembered the weight of a child's hand in his as he was showing a nurse how to set up an IV line. Then there was a sound—not an explosion exactly, but something that seemed to unmake the world. After that, the memories became pieces that would not cohere.

He knew the building had collapsed. He knew people had died. He knew he had been pulled from the rubble by someone whose face he could not recall. But when he tried to reconstruct what had happened in sequence, when he sat alone and forced himself to think through it step by step, the narrative would fracture. There were gaps—entire minutes missing, whole sections of the event that his mind simply would not hold. And more often than not, he found himself pushing the memory away before he could even attempt to assemble it, his mind recoiling from the effort as though the memory itself was dangerous.

What frightened him most was what the event had done to his understanding of everything. Before the bombing, Chukwu had believed in a comprehensible world—one where preparation mattered, where good intentions protected you, where medical training was a shield. He had believed he was the kind of person who could help, who could be steady in a crisis. Now he was certain that none of those things were true. The world was arbitrary and malevolent. He was not the person he had thought he was. He did not know who he was at all.

The triggers had emerged gradually over the weeks after he returned. Breathlessness came first—a sudden tightness in his chest that would arrive without warning, the sensation that his lungs could not expand, as though the weight of the collapsed building was pressing down on him again. It happened in the hospital corridors. It happened on the train. It happened in his apartment at three in the morning. The second trigger was silence. Absolute quiet—the kind that fell in a hospital stairwell, or in his own bedroom when the city traffic died down—would send him into a state of acute dread. Silence felt like the moment before catastrophe, the held breath before collapse. And violence of any kind, even on a television screen, would pull him back into a state of hyperalertness, his body rigid, his eyes scanning for threats.

He had begun avoiding the hospital. His supervisor had initially been understanding, but after three weeks of missed shifts, the conversations had shifted. There were other residents who could cover. There was a process for medical leave. The implication was clear: either return or withdraw. Chukwu had withdrawn. He had also stopped answering calls from his mother, stopped going to the clinic's weekly meetings, stopped leaving his apartment except to buy food. He was hypervigilant in his own home, attuned to every sound, every shift in the air pressure, certain that something was about to happen, that he needed to be ready. But ready for what, he could not have said.

It was his mother who had finally forced the issue. She had flown to Boston unannounced, let herself into his apartment, and found him sitting in the dark. She had cried. She had called a psychiatrist. And now, at twenty years old, Chukwu sat in a clinical office trying to explain to a stranger why the person he had become was someone he no longer recognized, and why the thought of returning to medicine—to the very thing he had built his life around—felt like walking back into a building that was still collapsing.
